newsitem.title: UK: ROWING-BRITAIN'S MEN MAKE GOOD SHOWING AT HENLEY.
newsitem.headline: ROWING-BRITAIN'S MEN MAKE GOOD SHOWING AT HENLEY.

text.p: Britain's top men rose to the challenge on finals day at Henley Royal Regatta on Sunday, with national crews winning three events and providing a good warm-up for next weekend's world cup finals in Lucerne, Switzerland.

The coxless four, containing Olympic gold medallists Steve Redgrave and Matthew Pinsent as well as bronze medallist Tim Foster and British international James Cracknell racing as Leander Club and Oxford University cruised home to an effortless two-and-a-half length victory in the Steward's Cup over a lightweight crew from Nottinghamshire County Rowing Association.
The four are currently leading the world cup standings, having won in Paris and Munich this year and say the boat is going "fairly well" at the moment.
But Redgrave, who has won four Olympic gold medals, was highly critical of the Regatta afterwards for not attracting good enough competition.
"I'm disappointed really, disappointed with the regatta as a whole," Redgrave said, adding the number of crews entered in his coxless fours event had been a letdown.
"To me it doesn't seem the same regatta."
The regatta, which started in 1839 and has always been an important date in the British social calendar has also been regarded as a leading international rowing event.

But it is losing its lustre. Last week, Bitish rowing official David Tanner said Henley needed more money to attract a higher quality of international crews if it wanted to move forward with the times.

A new pairing of Robert Thatcher and Ben Hunt-Davis from Leander Club, the same breeding ground as Redgrave and Pinsent, have taken over the coxless pairs mantle from the Olympic champions, winning easily over Germans Claas Fischer and Sebastian Franke in seven minutes 30 seconds.
The two are currently leading the world cup standings for the pairs, despite having come in second in the Munich and Paris world cup regattas.

"Comparisons to Pinsent and Redgrave are not something we talk about. We could never live up to them so we're not trying to, but if we keep going fast then we will keep racing in the pair," Hunt-Davis said.
"Lucerne will be very different to here because we were confident of winning and there everyone will be watching us and there are at least five or six good pairs racing."

Greg Searle, Olympic gold medallist in 1992 and bronze medallist in 1996, and who has now turned to the single sculls, beat Scotland's three times lightweight sculling world champion Peter Haining convincingly in the Diamond Sculls, but he has yet to make his mark on the event internationally.

Sweden's Maria Brandin, the current women's sculling world champion and defending Henley champion, did not seem troubled in a final against Britain's Guin Batten, with the race ending in a verdict of "not rowed out".

The Australian national eight, who won the world cup round in Paris earlier this year, looked strong against the eight from the Berliner Ruder-Club and Ruder Club Tegel in the final of the Grand Challenge Cup.
The Australians won by three lengths in 6 minutes 03 seconds.
